name: The Overjustification Effect
statement: Pay people for something they already loved doing, and their inner motivation for it can wither.
statementAccent: their inner motivation for it can wither
meaning: The overjustification effect is a phenomenon in which offering an expected external reward, such as money or a prize, for an activity a person already finds intrinsically rewarding can reduce their intrinsic motivation to do it. The external incentive over-justifies the behaviour, leading the person to attribute their action to the reward rather than to their own interest, so once the reward is removed their motivation can fall below where it started. The classic demonstration is a 1973 study by Mark Lepper, David Greene, and Richard Nisbett, in which preschool children who already enjoyed drawing were given a Good Player Award: those told in advance they would receive the award later spent less free time drawing than children who got an unexpected reward or none at all. Edward Deci's 1971 experiment paying people to solve puzzles found the same undermining of later voluntary engagement. The effect challenges the simple behaviourist assumption that rewards always strengthen behaviour.
mechanism: Two complementary theories explain the effect. Self-perception theory, associated with Daryl Bem, holds that people infer their own motives from their behaviour and its context: when a salient external reward is present, they conclude they acted for the reward rather than out of interest, so their sense of intrinsic motivation shrinks. Cognitive evaluation theory, part of Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory, holds that external rewards shift the perceived locus of causality from internal to external and undermine the feeling of autonomy that fuels intrinsic motivation. The undermining is specific: it occurs mainly for tangible, expected rewards given for tasks that are already intrinsically interesting. Unexpected rewards do not undermine motivation, because they cannot have been the reason for acting; verbal praise and positive feedback tend to enhance rather than reduce intrinsic motivation; and rewards for uninteresting tasks do not diminish motivation, since there was little intrinsic interest to lose. In the Good Player Award study, only the children promised the award in advance showed reduced later interest, confirming the role of the expected, salient incentive.

examples.text: Children promised an award for drawing later drew less in free play than those given an unexpected award or none, showing reduced intrinsic interest.
People paid to solve puzzles spent less free-choice time on them afterward than unpaid participants, as money undermined intrinsic motivation.
Unexpected rewards and verbal praise do not reduce intrinsic motivation, and praise can enhance it, marking the boundary of the effect.

variants.name: The self-perception account
variants.text: The explanation that a salient reward leads people to infer they acted for the reward rather than out of interest, lowering intrinsic motivation.

variants.name: The cognitive-evaluation account
variants.text: The self-determination-theory explanation that external rewards shift the locus of causality outward and undermine the autonomy that drives intrinsic motivation.

whyItMatters: The overjustification effect is a landmark finding in the psychology of motivation, with far-reaching implications for education, parenting, and management. It shows that rewards are not uniformly beneficial: paying or prizing people for activities they already enjoy can crowd out the intrinsic interest that sustained the behaviour, so incentive schemes may backfire once the rewards stop. This challenges the behaviourist assumption that reinforcement always strengthens behaviour and underlies self-determination theory's emphasis on autonomy, competence, and relatedness as sources of durable motivation. In practice it cautions against over-relying on grades, bonuses, and prizes for inherently engaging work, and it highlights the value of unexpected rewards and praise, which do not undermine motivation. The effect thus reshaped how psychologists and practitioners think about the relationship between external incentives and the inner drive to do things for their own sake.

working.text: identify an activity the person already finds rewarding for its own sake, so there is intrinsic motivation to affect.
offer a salient reward promised in advance for doing the activity, which becomes an external justification for the behaviour.
note that motivation can then fall below its original level, as the person now attributes the activity to the reward rather than their own interest.

limits: The overjustification effect has clear boundary conditions: it applies mainly to tangible, expected rewards for tasks that are already intrinsically interesting, while unexpected rewards, verbal praise, and rewards for dull tasks do not undermine and can even help. The strength of the effect is debated. A 1999 meta-analysis by Deci, Koestner, and Ryan supported the undermining of intrinsic motivation by such rewards, while an earlier analysis by Cameron and Pierce argued the effect is limited and largely inconsequential, and the two sides disputed each other's methods. The effect also appears stronger in children than adults, and some cited magnitudes come from secondary summaries. So while the phenomenon is well established within its boundary conditions, its size and generality remain contested, and rewards are not universally harmful to motivation.
misreadings: The effect does not show that rewards always reduce motivation; it applies to tangible, expected rewards for already-interesting tasks, while praise, unexpected rewards, and incentives for dull tasks do not undermine and may help. It is not that any payment ruins enjoyment, but that a salient external justification can crowd out intrinsic interest, especially when the reward is anticipated. And the effect's magnitude is debated, with meta-analyses reaching different conclusions, so treating overjustification as proof that all incentives backfire, or dismissing it as a myth, both overstate a real but bounded and contested phenomenon.
origin: Demonstrated by Mark Lepper, David Greene, and Richard Nisbett in their 1973 Good Player Award study and by Edward Deci's 1971 puzzle experiment, and explained through self-perception theory and Deci and Ryan's cognitive evaluation theory.
